patch.value: The immutable history op vocabulary is ungoverned: 71 op literals across five naming conventions, with the same operation spelled two ways in one file, are written permanently with no enum, no contract, and no gate

Every mutating action writes an entry whose op field names the operation. That name is the primary key analytics, replay, redaction, compaction and any external verifier read to understand what happened. It is written into an append-only stream that the project promises never to alter. Nothing declares what those names may be.

Census measured on this repository at 2026.7.28:

- 71 distinct op string literals exist in src. There is no enum, no union type, no constant table, and no contract entry for any of them. The only central reference is a projection format string.
- 37 distinct op values are already permanently recorded across 40,343 entries in 2,155 streams.
- At least five naming conventions are in simultaneous use: bare verbs (create, close, claim, release, append, delete, import, investigate); snake_case compounds (comment_add, files_add, docs_add, note_add, learning_add, history_compact, history_compact_baseline, plan_add_step, files_discover); a colon-namespaced snake form (gc:lock_remove, gc:checkpoint_remove, gc:transaction_journal_remove, init:ensure_dir, init:runtime_schema_file, reindex:embeddings, lock:release); a colon-namespaced kebab form (history:author-acknowledge, profile:apply-fields, profile:apply-statuses, profile:apply-types, schema:add-field, schema:add-status, schema:add-type, schema:apply-preset); a colon SUFFIX namespace (create:history, delete:history, import:history, restore:history, history_redact:history, history_repair:history); and one dotted form (pm.command).
- Number agreement is inconsistent within one family: files_add, docs_add and tests_add are plural while note_add, comment_add and learning_add are singular, for the same add-an-annotation shape.
- Proof that this is drift and not design: src/sdk/init.ts writes op "init:type-preset" at line 565 and op "init:type_preset" at line 1029. The same operation is spelled two ways in the same file. Whichever path runs, the spelling is immutable from that moment.
- history:author-acknowledge is the only recorded op using the colon-kebab form, and 9 entries already carry it permanently.

Consequence: any consumer of the immutable record - a replay tool, an external auditor, a metrics job, a future format reader across the decades the format claims to cover - must special-case an open-ended vocabulary that no gate constrains. A new op name cannot be reviewed against a rule because no rule is written down. The record is immutable, so every drifted name is permanent and the cost of the gap only accumulates.

This is the same class as the dependency-kind lexicon and the flag lexicon and the error-code catalog, one layer deeper: those govern surfaces a caller can re-read, this governs a record nobody can ever rewrite. Scope is the op vocabulary only. Entry presence is a different concern and stays with the history-completeness gate. Entry ordering identity stays with its own owner.

A single declared source enumerates every permitted history op name, and every write site derives its op from that source rather than a literal; A naming grammar for op names is written down and machine-checked, so a non-conforming op cannot reach a stream; The init type-preset duplicate spelling is resolved to one name and the historical entries carrying the retired spelling are documented as a known legacy alias rather than rewritten; The declared vocabulary is published through the runtime contract surface so an external replay or verification tool can enumerate it without reading source; A gate fails when a new op literal appears that is absent from the declared vocabulary

value.text: Sibling class measured 2026-07-29 in the same record this item censuses: the author field of the same 41,021 entries holds 477 distinct spellings with no enumeration, no contract entry and no gate, and four of its six most frequent values are two harnesses written two ways. It is the same ungoverned-value-domain shape as the 71 op literals, one layer harder for the same reason - the stream is append-only, so neither vocabulary can be fixed by migration and both need read-time canonicalization against declared data. Owner for the author half is pm-3yxwv5; keep the two separate because the op vocabulary is written only by the product while the author vocabulary is also written by callers through --author and PM_AUTHOR.

value.text: Live op census, 2026-08-01, over all 2,258 history streams and 42,771 entries. 37 distinct op literals are actually written: update 10,931, comment_add 8,010, files_add 6,592, tests_add 3,086, claim 2,745, release 2,281, create 2,215, close 2,202, docs_add 1,431, test_run_track 913, note_add 725, learning_add 636, update_audit 309, update_ownership_bypass 120, append 115, plan_complete_step 85, plan_add_step 71, plan_update_step 44, history_repair 42, history_compact_baseline 41, history_compact 41, history_redact 23, plan_create_metadata 19, history:author-acknowledge 9, plan_create_initial_step 12, plan_append_discovery 12, delete 12, plan_append_validation 9, plan_append_decision 7, plan_approve 6, plan_link_step 4, comment_edit 4, comment_delete 3, plan_unlink_step 1, plan_reorder_step 1, note_delete 1. The naming-convention finding is confirmed and is now a single outlier: history:author-acknowledge is the one colon-namespaced literal in the entire immutable record; every other op is snake_case, and the plan_* family is the one that uses a namespace prefix without a separator. That makes the canonicalization tractable -- one recorded spelling has to move, not a class of them. The gap between 37 written and ~71 declared is also the measurement pm-pww8ax needs: half the declared vocabulary has never been exercised on a real workspace.
